g.text: A for-loop over 300 sockets is a machine for transferring money to whoever is first
Which is why 'every subscriber receives the update at the same instant' is a technical constraint, not an ethics statement.
Unicast TCP - one write per subscriber, in a loop
for s in subscribers: # 300 iterations
socket[s].write(update) # 1-5 us of syscall + kernel work EACH

Subscriber 1 knows the new price while subscriber 300 is still acting on a stale
view - so subscriber 1 can trade against subscriber 300's resting orders at prices
that are no longer correct, and profit systematically from POSITION IN A LOOP.
An implementation detail nobody agreed to, and in most jurisdictions the VENUE's
problem rather than the participant's.
Multicast - ONE datagram, replicated in hardware
publisher
switch fabric
subscriber 1
subscriber 2
subscriber 300
duplicates the packet in HARDWARE
at each branch point
ALL 300 subscribers - remaining skew is cable length and NIC processing
tens of NANOSECONDS. Physics, not software.
The three modes, since they get asked as a set: unicast for order entry (each broker's own
orders and fills - must be private), multicast for market data, broadcast unused because it
cannot be scoped to subscribers. Anycast is for geographic routing and does not apply.
Multicast means UDP - and a dropped update leaves a subscriber with a WRONG book, not a slow one
sequence number on every message
a subscriber that receives 10,041 after
10,039 knows 10,040 is missing - at once,
with no round trip to ask.
NAK, never ACK
subscribers report only what is MISSING.
Acking every message from 300 subscribers
is 300x the reverse traffic - and a
per-subscriber loop all over again.
retransmit on a UNICAST channel
deliberately off the main path, so one
subscriber's packet loss cannot slow
anybody else's delivery.
periodic full snapshots
interleaved with the deltas, so a
subscriber 50,000 messages behind (or
newly connected) resyncs from snapshot +
deltas, not 50,000 retransmit requests.
The concession worth stating out loud: retransmission is INHERENTLY UNFAIR - whoever dropped a packet gets it later than
everyone else. Accepted, because the alternative (hold every subscriber until the slowest acknowledges) makes the whole feed's
latency equal to the WORST subscriber's latency - worse for everyone, and unfair in a less obvious way. The rule is: the
PRIMARY path must be simultaneous; recovery is best-effort.
Three depths - the difference is real, not packaging
L1 best bid and ask only
MSFT bid 415.00 x 1,200
It is the bestLevel pointer, so it is
cheap to produce and cheap to ship.
Sufficient for most retail use.
L2 aggregated depth by price level
MSFT BIDS ASKS
Each level's totalVolume, maintained
incrementally - so it is O(depth), not
O(orders). Shows the SHAPE of liquidity:
how far a large order moves the price.
L3 every individual queued order
^ FIFO queue position, VISIBLE
Exposes the queue position that price-time
priority depends on, so a participant can
see where they stand. Highest bandwidth by
a wide margin - and where iceberg orders
get awkward, since hidden quantity must
not appear.
Candlesticks are DERIVED, not published from the book: the publisher builds them from the EXECUTION stream, because only
actual trades count, not quotes. Many intervals (1s, 1m, 5m, 1h, 1d) are maintained in parallel from that one stream.
The publisher takes 215,000 executions/sec and must not allocate
class CandlestickChart:
sticks: Candlestick[N] # PRE-ALLOCATED, fixed size
head: int # newest; release-store
tail: int # oldest; overwritten on wrap
no allocation at runtime a malloc in a 215k/sec path is an unbounded-latency
event and a GC trigger - the same discipline as the engine
bounded memory the ring overwrites the oldest entry; older candles were
already persisted off-path by the reporter
lock-free, 1 writer / N readers readers acquire-load head and read up to head - 1,
so a torn view of the newest entry is never observed
And the classic: pad head and tail onto SEPARATE CACHE LINES. Sharing a 64-byte line means the writer's store to head
invalidates that line in every reader's cache - FALSE SHARING - costing up to an order of magnitude in throughput even though
the two variables are logically independent. A one-line fix for a bug that is invisible in the code and obvious in a profiler.
Failover is a permission change, not a state transfer
the sequenced event stream - (epoch, sequence) stamped on every event
PRIMARY engine
processes AND publishes
STANDBY engine
processes, publishes NOTHING
Not warming up and not idle - fully caught up at ALL TIMES, processing every event
the primary does and maintaining a byte-identical book. Which works only because
matching is deterministic: same inputs, same sequence, therefore same state.
Primary and standby differ in exactly ONE thing: whether they publish. Both
compute; one speaks. So promotion is not a state transfer - it is a flag flip, and
it completes in the time it takes to detect the failure.
Fencing - because the failure that matters is a primary that APPEARS dead and is not
A GC pause, a partition or a slow disk makes a healthy primary miss heartbeats. Promote the
standby, the old primary resumes publishing, and now TWO engines publish conflicting fills
for the same orders - both internally consistent, and unreconcilable. So leadership is a
LEASE WITH AN EPOCH: every published event carries (epoch, sequence), consumers track the
highest epoch seen and REJECT anything lower, and a promotion increments it.
A deposed primary keeps processing into its own memory harmlessly - it
simply cannot be heard. Same pattern as the message queue's leader_epoch
and the wallet's phase-status CAS, and the reason is always identical:
'I am the leader' is a claim that EXPIRES, and a monotonic epoch is what
makes expiry checkable by the RECIPIENT rather than trusted from the
claimant.
99.99% is 8.6 seconds a trading day - so the layers, and the row that inverts the usual instinct
failure
response
recovery time
a process on the primary box dies
hot standby process promoted, same box
microseconds - milliseconds
the primary box dies
warm standby BOX promoted; stream replicated to it by reliable UDP
seconds
the datacenter dies
standby datacenter; TRADING HALTS, resumes after a formal restart
minutes - hours, with a halt
leadership is UNCERTAIN
HALT the affected symbols
deliberate unavailability
That last row is the design's most important reliability decision. Halting a symbol is embarrassing, publicly visible and
costs money. Publishing two divergent books means fills that do not reconcile and positions that do not exist - and it is
UNFIXABLE AFTER THE FACT, because you cannot un-tell a broker that their order filled. When you cannot be sure who is
authoritative, being UNAVAILABLE is strictly better than being WRONG.
Why not multi-region: a cross-region round trip is 150 ms, four
orders of magnitude over the budget - but the deeper objection is
conceptual. An exchange IS a single authoritative ordering of events
per symbol, and that is precisely what geographic distribution cannot
provide. Two regions accepting orders independently produce two
orderings, and reconciling them means deciding retroactively whose
trades happened. So DR is a standby datacenter for resuming after a
catastrophe, never active-active - and a regional disaster means a
trading halt.
And the honest gap: colocation sells the right to be physically closer to the multicast source, partially undoing this
module's fairness work. The defence - stated as a defence, not as fairness - is that the advantage is BOUNDED (metres of
cable, not unbounded software), OPENLY PRICED (anyone can buy it) and DISCLOSED, unlike the unicast loop's invisible,
unpriced advantage determined by an arbitrary iteration order. Better, and not the same thing as simultaneous delivery.
